analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicaid to cover home-based attendant care so disabled and older people can avoid nursing homes.
analysis.headline: Despite 18 cosponsors including one Republican, the bill never received a committee markup or floor vote; it sat in the Senate Finance Committee until the Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every state's Medicaid program to cover attendant services — help with dressing, bathing, meals, and daily tasks — for Medicaid beneficiaries who qualify for nursing home care but choose to live at home instead. The bill's own findings note that Medicaid long-term care spending is heavily tilted toward institutions: only about a third of long-term care dollars pay for home and community-based services, and nursing home care is the only long-term care service federal law guarantees in every state. It offered states extra federal money for moving early and for transition activities, plus grants to rebuild their long-term care systems around community living.
analysis.who_benefits: People with disabilities and older Americans on Medicaid who need nursing-home-level care but want to live in their own homes, with family, or in their communities. Family caregivers gain relief and support, and home care workers gain new jobs and, under the bill's grant programs, investments in their skills, earnings, and career prospects.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Disabled and older Medicaid beneficiaries, families, home care workers

how_it_helps.text: Makes community-based attendant services a mandatory Medicaid benefit statewide for anyone who qualifies for nursing facility care and chooses home-based services, instead of the patchwork of uneven state options that existed.
Bases eligibility on the level of care a person needs — not their age or type of disability — so working-age adults with disabilities, children, and older Americans all qualify.

Gives states an enhanced federal match for moving early, plus up to 10 extra percentage points of federal funding for transition and diversion activities, and pays 70 to 90 percent of the federal share for community-based services above a cost benchmark.

Authorizes $50 million a year in grants for fiscal 2006 through 2008 to help states shift their systems toward community living, with a Consumer Task Force majority-controlled by people with disabilities.
Requires states to build quality safeguards into home-based care, including abuse and neglect reporting, external monitoring, consumer surveys, and provider sanctions.

analysis.who_pays: The federal government and state Medicaid programs bear the cost of the new mandatory benefit and the enhanced federal matching rates. Nursing facilities would lose residents and revenue as people move home. State governments also accept a maintenance-of-effort requirement barring them from cutting other services for people with disabilities and the elderly to pay for the new benefit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal and state Medicaid budgets; nursing facilities

drawbacks.text: The bill creates a new mandatory federal entitlement with enhanced federal matching rates, adding real and open-ended spending to Medicaid at federal and state expense.
States must commit to the benefit by October 1, 2009 and accept a maintenance-of-effort rule that locks in existing spending on disability and elderly services, limiting state budget flexibility.

A fair objection is that home-based care is harder to monitor for quality and safety than institutional care; the bill answers this with mandatory abuse reporting, external monitoring, and provider sanctions, but oversight of scattered home settings is a genuine challenge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The upside is large and concrete: it would give people who qualify for nursing homes a real choice to live at home, ending a federal rule that effectively forces institutional care as the only guaranteed option. The costs — new federal and state spending and a state maintenance-of-effort requirement — are real but were partly offset by enhanced federal matching designed to ease the transition, and the bill's own findings suggest community care can cost less than institutional care for many people. The main design risk is quality oversight in home settings, which the bill addresses at length rather than ignores.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced on February 16, 2005 and referred the same day to the Senate Finance Committee, the bill never received a markup or vote and died when that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Harkin introduced the bill with 11 original cosponsors including Republican Arlen Specter, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance on February 16, 2005.
Eighteen senators cosponsored the bill: 17 Democrats and 1 Republican.

The bill's findings document the institutional bias it targeted: only about 33 percent of Medicaid long-term care funds paid for home and community-based care, and nursing home care was the only long-term care service federally guaranteed in every state.
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral — the bill sat in the Finance Committee until the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nursing facilities kept the status quo in which institutional care remains the only federally guaranteed long-term care option, and federal and state Medicaid budgets avoided the cost of the new mandatory benefit. People with disabilities who wanted to move out of institutions gained nothing from this outcome.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: Arlen Specter
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as one of its two original sponsors from the floor, the only Republican cosponsor.

for.name: ADAPT
for.what_they_did: Ran a years-long grassroots campaign for this legislation (known as MiCASSA), organizing members with disabilities to press Congress for the right to receive long-term care at home.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee the bill was referred to; the record shows the committee took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress — no hearing or markup.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over Medicaid
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on February 16, 2005 and never reported it out.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never got a vote, so there is no roll-call to measure; its support was heavily Democratic — 17 Democratic cosponsors to 1 Republican — though the sole Republican was a high-ranking senator who signed on as an original cosponsor.

industries.industry: Nursing facilities and institutional long-term care providers
industries.note: The bill ends nursing home care's status as the only federally guaranteed long-term care service and pays states to shift Medicaid dollars to home and community-based care, moving residents out of facilities. Facilities stood to lose the captive clientele that current law guarantees them.

industries.industry: Home care agencies and attendant workers
industries.note: A new mandatory Medicaid benefit creates a large pool of covered customers for community-based attendant services, and the bill's grants fund worker recruitment, training, earnings, and career development. Consumers themselves could also hire and manage their own attendants outside agencies.

States take on a new mandatory benefit and a maintenance-of-effort requirement, but receive enhanced federal matching rates, up to 90 percent federal payment for some community-care expenditures, and $50 million a year in systems-change grants. The federal incentives were designed to make the shift budget-neutral or better for early-moving states.
